objective: By the end of this lesson you can give a simulated engine failure that stays safe, teach best glide, wind, energy and field selection so they stick, explain ELT and ATC help, and spot and fix a learner's forced landing errors while you demonstrate from the right seat.
why: Simulated engine failures done wrong have created real emergencies and caused accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], so the instructor's setup matters as much as the learner's flying. Powerplant failure and fuel problems are among the top four causes of fatal general aviation accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], and many real emergency landings could have been prevented by habits built in training [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. What you teach here is what your learner will do on the worst day of their flying life.

prereading.what: How an instructor gives simulated emergency landings: throttle, field selection, corrections, keeping the engine warm, throttle control and when to end it.
prereading.label: AFH 9-28 to 9-29

prereading.what: Glide ratio, best glide and minimum sink, weight, drag and wind, teaching the normal glide by sound and feel, gliding turns and the common glide errors.
prereading.label: AFH 3-21 to 3-24

prereading.what: Types of emergency landing, psychological hazards, energy at touchdown, terrain selection, configuration and approach planning.
prereading.label: AFH 18-1 to 18-5

prereading.what: The airplane as an energy system: throttle as total energy control, elevator as the exchanger.
prereading.label: AFH 4-1 to 4-4

prereading.what: Power-off approaches, the key position, wind and base leg placement, and power-off accuracy errors.
prereading.label: AFH 9-25 to 9-27

prereading.what: Asking for help early, radar help, code 7700, intercept and escort, ELT types, testing and false alarms.
prereading.label: AIM 6-1-1 to 6-2-4

prereading.what: Instructional risks, including simulated engine failures, and how to manage risk while teaching maneuvers.
prereading.label: AIH 10-7 to 10-8

warmup: Think first: your private pilot learner has flown six simulated engine failures with you, and every time she found a lovely hayfield and made it with altitude to spare. Today she reaches for the restart checklist before she has picked a field, and the airspeed decays 15 knots. What is she telling you about her training so far, what would you say right now, and what would you change about the next six failures you give her?

key_terms.def: Practice the instructor starts by retarding the throttle and calling "simulated emergency landing"; it can begin in any configuration [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
The speed that gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air, at the highest lift-to-drag ratio [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
The speed that keeps the airplane in the air longest; slower than best glide, less distance, not often published [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Distance traveled compared with altitude lost; 10,000 feet forward for 1,000 feet down is 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
A stabilized, power-off descent at best glide speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
A glide flown at a speed other than best glide; it can miss the spot, float, overrun or stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
A convenient point in the air, chosen for the altitude and wind, from which the pilot judges the rest of the power-off approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
The total energy stored as altitude and airspeed and how it is split between them [[24:87|AFH 4-1]] [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].
The throttle: it sets thrust against drag and so adds or removes total energy [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].
Opening the throttle briefly during a long power-off glide to keep the engine warm; the AFH asks for it on every simulated emergency landing [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt your position, fuel, weather or anything else that affects safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
A digital ELT detected and decoded by the Cospas-Sarsat satellites; it must be registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

chunks.title: Setting up a simulated failure that stays safe

body.p: Start with the rule you will be tested under. The evaluator will not request a simulated powerplant failure in a single-engine airplane unless a safe landing can be completed (ACS Appendix 2), and for this Task the execution must allow a safe landing if the engine really quits (ACS Appendix 3). Hold yourself to the same rule with every learner.

How the AFH does it: the instructor retards the throttle and calls "simulated emergency landing" [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. The AFH gives the purpose: to build accuracy, judgment, planning, procedures and confidence when little or no power is available [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Retarding the throttle is the only method the handbooks describe for a single-engine airplane. The AFH mentions the mixture only for a simulated failure during a multiengine takeoff roll [[24:284|AFH 13-35]]; nothing describes shutting off the mixture, fuel or magnetos to simulate a single-engine failure (see gaps).

head: Before you pull the power
What the sources say
rows: Where

Over terrain where a safe landing is possible (ACS Appendix 2). Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no one may fly below an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property if the engine fails [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]
Congested areas
1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]
Elsewhere
500 feet above the surface; over open water or sparsely populated areas, no closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]
How low
End it as soon as you can tell whether a safe landing is assured, and never so low that it creates undue hazard or annoyance to people or property on the ground [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Carburetor ice
If icing is suspected, full carburetor heat on before the throttle closes [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Traffic
Clear the area in the direction of turns and descent; failing to do so is the first glide error the AFH lists [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Throttle
Agree who has complete control of the throttle; confusion has caused many near accidents [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]

callout.text: Simulated engine failures, if performed incorrectly, can and have created real emergencies and caused accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. A cold engine that will not take power at the bottom of the glide turns a lesson into the real thing.

body.p: Application: the property rows above are why you pick the practice area before you pull the power. The approach ends as a go-around, not a landing, so plan the termination well clear of houses, livestock and people.

callout.text: Before a ground reference maneuver, the AIH suggests asking the learner to name collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The same prompt fits any practice area (application).

check.q: What is the only method the AFH gives an instructor for starting a simulated emergency landing in a single-engine airplane?
check.a: Retard the throttle and call "simulated emergency landing" [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

body.p: Entry: if the failure comes above best glide, the pilot lets the airplane slow (even climbs) to best glide, then lowers the nose and trims; at or below best glide, the nose goes down at once. Flaps and gear go to the proper configuration for the situation [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. To enter, hold altitude with back pressure while the speed decays, because the nose tends to drop as the slipstream over the tail decreases [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

Immediate action items are flown from memory, then the full procedure is found quickly [[24:348|AFH 17-14]]. The ACS accepts that reading a checklist may be impractical in some phases; the evaluator then looks for the memory items, followed by a checklist review once conditions permit (ACS Appendix 2).

The critical items to check are the fuel selector and the fuel in that tank, fuel pressure (is the electric pump needed?), mixture, magneto switch and carburetor heat. Many actual emergency landings came from a selector on an empty tank while the other was full, so switching tanks can be wise even when the gauges show fuel [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The AFH sample restart list runs airspeed, carburetor heat on, fuel selector both, mixture rich, ignition both (or START if the propeller has stopped), primer in and locked [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The Commercial lesson (CA.IX.B) walks through each item; here the job is teaching the habit.

bullets: Each step is called out to the instructor, and a checklist is strongly recommended; most manufacturers provide one [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

The simulated steps may differ somewhat from those in a real emergency [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Say before the flight which items the learner will touch and name and which, if any, will actually be moved (application).

Combining the checklist with picking a field and flying the approach is hard early in training; the goal is a habit so strong that a real failure gets the restart items checked while the field is chosen [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Your POH/AFM wins over the AFH whenever they differ [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

callout.text: Glide, field, checklist, call. Fly first; positive control on final has priority over configuration and checklist tasks [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

check.q: Your learner reaches for the checklist before setting the glide attitude. What order should she use?
check.a: Set best glide and trim first [[24:199|AFH 9-28]], then the memory items and checklist; airplane control has priority [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

body.p: Importance of best glide speed and its relationship to distance (K2a): best glide gives the greatest forward distance for the altitude lost in still air, because it occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio. Fly faster or slower and drag rises, so the glide ratio drops and the distance shrinks [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

bullets: Weight does not change the glide angle or the distance if the proper speed is flown; a heavier airplane needs a higher speed and gets there sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Drag items (flaps, gear, cowl flaps) force a lower nose to hold speed and shorten the glide; remove them if possible for maximum distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
The cardinal rule: never stretch a glide with back pressure below best glide. It lands you short and can stall you [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
In a glide, slight left rudder is likely needed and larger control deflections, because the design compensation for p-factor and slipstream remains when they disappear [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

body.p: Why it must become automatic: glides are flown more subconsciously than other maneuvers, because in a forced landing most attention goes to other details [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Teaching it: have the learner memorize the attitude against the horizon, the sound of the air and the feel of the controls. Point out that rising sound means rising speed. Teach all three cues (sound, visual, pressure) consciously until experience builds, and teach abnormal glides only after the normal glide is solid [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: ACS standard you demonstrate to, and that your private and commercial learners meet: "Establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed, ±10 knots" (ACS AI.XII.B.S1, PA.IX.B.S1, CA.IX.B.S1). Recommended means the POH/AFM number.

check.q: Your learner glides 15 knots above best glide 'to get there sooner.' What happens to the distance?
check.a: Drag rises above best glide, so the glide ratio drops and the airplane lands shorter [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

head: Sub-item
What to teach
Source
rows: Difference between best glide speed and minimum sink speed (K2b)

Best glide covers the most distance; minimum sink keeps you up longest, at a lower speed, losing altitude at the lowest rate but covering less distance. Minimum sink is not often published and is generally a few knots below best glide. Use it when time matters more than distance, such as ditching at sea
Effects of wind on glide distance (K2c)
A tailwind carries the airplane farther because of the higher groundspeed; a headwind shortens the glide
Wind at touchdown

Groundspeed is the most critical factor in how hard you stop: double it and the destructive energy is four times as great. Touch down at the lowest possible controllable airspeed, using all available aerodynamic devices

body.p: Reading the wind: teach learners to estimate direction and speed from windsocks, smoke, dust, brush fires, wind farms and patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. On a power-off approach, the crab needed on base also shows the wind [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

Placing the base leg: the stronger the headwind on final, the closer the base leg, so the glide to the field is steeper over the ground [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. In a headwind a slightly faster speed than best glide can help stabilize the rest of the approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

callout.text: Tailwind to get there, headwind to land. Wind helps the glide one way and the touchdown the other (application of [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] and [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]).

A good demonstration: give the same simulated failure twice from the same altitude, once heading downwind and once into the wind, and let the learner see how much farther the downwind glide reaches over the ground (application).

check.q: Why does the memory aid say 'tailwind to get there, headwind to land'?
check.a: A tailwind raises groundspeed and stretches the glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], but at touchdown groundspeed sets the destructive energy, which grows with its square [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

body.p: Carburetor ice is the atmospheric effect most tied to this Task, because a simulated failure means a long time at closed throttle. With the throttle closed the engine cools quickly, the fuel vaporizes less completely and icing becomes more likely [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. In a fixed-pitch airplane the first sign is a drop in rpm, which may be followed by roughness, and the chart is a guide only: icing is possible in conditions it does not show [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

bullets: Before closing the throttle in icing conditions, put the carburetor heat full on and leave it on; open the throttle smoothly for a few seconds now and then to keep the engine warm, or the heater may not supply enough heat [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Partial heat, or heat used for too short a time, can make icing worse [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

Thin air: on a hot, humid day or at altitude, the airplane needs more true airspeed for the same angle of attack [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]]. It lands at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed, so the landing distance grows [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Wind and gusts: see the wind chunk. A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21 percent to landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Snow and smooth water can take away depth perception; a snow landing is made like a ditching [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

Night: a forced landing may bring terrain hazards you cannot see, and an alternator failure can take the electrical system with it [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. The AFH suggests a landing area close to public access, to help rescue [[24:230|AFH 11-13]].
Haze and pollution restrict visibility and make collision hazards worse in training areas [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

callout.text: Use the carburetor icing chart in the preflight briefing: read the temperature and humidity of the day and let the learner decide whether carburetor heat goes on before you pull the power [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

check.q: Today's temperature and humidity fall outside the chart's high icing box. Does that rule out carburetor ice?
check.a: No. The chart shows where ice is most likely; icing is possible in conditions it does not show [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

chunks.title: Energy management and a stabilized glide

body.p: Total mechanical energy is potential energy from altitude (mgh) plus kinetic energy from airspeed (one half mV squared) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. The throttle is the total energy controller; the elevator is the energy distribution controller that trades altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

Teach the failure with this picture. When the engine quits, the throttle valve is shut: thrust is gone, drag keeps draining energy, and the elevator can only move what is left between the two tanks. Excess airspeed at the failure is stored energy that can be turned into distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Every slip, flap and turn only decides how fast the rest drains (application).

bullets: Hold one gliding speed; changing it ruins every judgment of glide distance and landing spot [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Use any mix of straight glides and spirals to arrive at the key position at normal pattern altitude for the field; from there it is a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Starting with the same energy each time makes power-off approaches more predictable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

To stabilize the rest of a power-off approach, the AFH lists S-turns, slips, early or late flaps, a speed below best glide, or slightly above best glide in a headwind [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. That is different from stretching a glide to reach a spot, which it forbids [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

A stabilized approach is a constant-angle path to a chosen point at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Focus on its elements rather than insisting on every criterion [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; with no engine, the power item does not apply.
Plan to be slightly high and delay full flaps until they cannot make you short [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
A sink rate over 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive; do not dive at the aiming point [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

callout.text: Mismanaged energy is a factor in the three most common fatal accident types: loss of control in flight, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

check.q: Which stabilized approach criterion does not fit a power-off glide, and what does the AFH say about meeting every criterion?
check.a: The power setting item; the AFH says to focus on the elements rather than insist on all the criteria [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Choosing the field and sticking with it

body.p: The choice of sites depends on the route chosen in preflight planning, the height above the ground, and excess airspeed [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Choosing the route wisely is part of preflight risk analysis, because an engine failure makes nearby airports and terrain supremely important [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. The goal of AFH chapter 18 is that almost any terrain can be suitable for a survivable crash landing if the pilot uses the airplane structure for protection [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

head: Consideration
What the learner should weigh
rows: Altitude
High up, choose the general area first and the exact spot later, since terrain from altitude can mislead [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]
Wind
Wind direction and speed are the first of three factors in planning the approach [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]
Terrain
Dimensions and slope of the field [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]; dense crops and brush absorb energy well [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]
Obstructions
Obstacles on final; roads usually have wires alongside, so watch for the poles [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]
Gliding distance
Overestimating the glide tempts a pilot to stretch it over obstacles; an approach over open ground regardless of wind can be better [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]
Available landing distance
Very little stopping distance is needed if the deceleration is uniform [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]; a confined spot that needs a steep descent is a trap [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]

body.p: With more fields to choose from at higher altitudes, inexperienced pilots tend to put off the decision, and errors in maneuvering and glide estimation creep in [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Once a field is chosen, the learner points it out to the instructor [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Altitude, obstructions, wind direction, landing direction, surface and gradient, and the airplane's landing distance decide the pattern and approach to fly [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

callout.text: Practice field selection all the time, not only after a power cut. "Identify a field suitable for a forced landing" is one of the AIH's examples of a distraction task [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

body.p: Terrain types (trees, water, roads, crops) are covered in the Private and Commercial lessons (PA.IX.B, CA.IX.B).
Following or changing the planned flightpath (R2):

Normally the learner plans and flies a pattern to the first field chosen until the instructor ends the simulation. That gives you a chance to explain and correct errors, and gives the learner a chance to see the results of them [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

If the learner sees during the approach that the field would obviously end in disaster, and a better one is within gliding distance, permit the change. Then explain the hazards of last-minute decisions, such as excessive maneuvering at very low altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

bullets: As a rule, change your mind only once. A well-flown crash landing in poor terrain can be less hazardous than an uncontrolled touchdown on a good field [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Corrections to stress for a misjudged height or glide angle: slips, flaps, moving the base leg, and changing the turn onto final [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
The key position is not a landmark. Learners who tie it to a tree or a crossroad are lost when that object is missing, so vary the altitude and location as much as practical [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

callout.text: Low and late field changes bring steep, uncoordinated turns near the ground, the setup for the spin described in the low-altitude chunk [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

check.q: Which variables does the AFH say decide the pattern and approach to the chosen field?
check.a: Altitude, obstructions, wind direction, landing direction, landing surface and gradient, and the airplane's landing distance [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

bullets: Glide: remove drag items if possible for the most distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
After a complete power failure, hold best glide until you must reconfigure for landing, and plan a steeper approach than usual [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Final: flaps are recommended when time permits, because they lower stall speed and help at slow speed, but premature flaps waste altitude and can wreck a sound plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Retractable gear: no hard and fast rule; follow the AFM/POH [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Electrical: turning it off before touchdown lowers the fire risk, but leave the master on while you still need power for vital systems such as electric flaps [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

A rough engine: use whatever power it gives, but it is generally better to switch engine and fuel off just before touchdown; that keeps the pilot in charge, and a cooled engine cuts the fire hazard [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

body.p: Prepare for landing as specified by the evaluator (S5). On the checkride, and with your own learners, agree before the flight how each simulation ends: the termination point, a go-around or a landing at an airport, and which forced landing items are only touched and named (application). The sample checklist ends with mixture idle cutoff, fuel off, ignition off, flaps, master off, doors unlatched, touchdown slightly tail low and heavy braking [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

Recovery from the simulation: in simulated power failure training, apply power as the 10 percent lead value appears on the altimeter, slowly but positively, while raising the nose and retrimming [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

If the simulation ends with a real landing at an airport: aiming at the runway numbers leaves no safety cushion, so pick a point farther down [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. A good landing away from the spot beats a poor one on it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]], and forcing the airplane on to avoid overshooting the spot is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

callout.text: In a retractable, failure to lower the gear and premature flap or gear extension are both listed power-off approach errors [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Watch the gear when the approach ends in a go-around or in a real landing at an airport.

check.q: Why does the AFH prefer switching the engine and fuel off just before touchdown, even when the engine still gives some power?
check.a: It keeps the pilot in charge of the touchdown, and a cooled engine reduces the fire hazard [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

chunks.title: ATC services to aircraft in distress

body.p: Teach learners that declaring an emergency is an appropriate reaction, and that ATC then gives priority handling [[25:24|AIH 1-20]]. In an emergency needing immediate action the PIC may deviate from part 91 rules as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot doubts position, fuel, weather or anything else that affects safety, and a pilot who becomes apprehensive for any reason should ask for help at once [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Help can come informally, by calling the facility with the problem, intentions and help wanted, but the ICAO distress and urgency procedures have decided advantages [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

head: Service
What the AIM says
rows: Radar help for VFR aircraft
Vectors when you can talk to the controller and are in radar coverage; the help is advisory and the pilot stays responsible for flying safely [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]
Transponder

7700 with Mode C triggers an alarm at all control positions; keep squawking even if outside radar coverage [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. If already in contact on an assigned code, keep it unless told otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]
Intercept and escort
SAR aircraft can escort an aircraft in difficulty to a safe landing, normally at the nearest adequate airport; the pilot may refuse it [[34:29|AIM 6-2-3]]
Frequencies

The frequency in use first; otherwise 121.5 MHz, guarded by direction finding stations, most civil towers and radar facilities. If an ARTCC does not answer on 121.5, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Distress words
MAYDAY, preferably three times, has absolute priority and commands radio silence [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
After contact
Comply, cooperate, and do not change frequency unless absolutely necessary [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]

body.p: The distress message has a preferred order, from MAYDAY to the number of people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. You will put it in order in a game later.

callout.text: In practice, have the learner say the distress call and the 7700 squawk aloud without transmitting or setting them (application). The words come faster on the real day when they have been said many times.

check.q: Besides an informal call stating the problem, intentions and help wanted, why does the AIM prefer the ICAO distress and urgency procedures?
check.a: They have decided advantages over the informal call [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

head: Topic
Rule or fact
rows: Types
Analog ELTs transmit on 121.5 and 243.0 MHz; 406 MHz units are digital, can carry owner and position data, and must be registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Registration

If a registered 406 MHz ELT goes off, the rescue coordination center can contact the owner to check the airplane's status, so a search of a hangared airplane is avoided; 406 MHz units also send a stronger signal [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Detection

Satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 and 243.0 MHz in 2009, so analog ELTs depend on a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. SAR can respond to a 406 MHz alert in minutes, against possibly hours for 121.5 [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Homing
406 MHz ELTs also carry a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter for the final search phase [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Other locating devices
Pilots who do not own the airplane should check its ELT and, as appropriate, carry a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Activation
ELTs transmit for at least 48 hours once activated; pilots and passengers should know how to activate one by hand and verify it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Testing
Analog units only in the first 5 minutes after the hour, no more than three sweeps; airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
False alarms
Monitor 121.5 before engine shutdown at the end of each flight [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]

body.p: 14 CFR 91.207 requires an approved personal or automatic ELT for most part 91 airplanes [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]], and fixed and deployable automatic types are attached as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]]. Batteries are replaced or recharged after more than 1 cumulative hour of use or when 50 percent of their useful life has expired [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]], and the ELT is inspected within 12 calendar months for installation, battery corrosion, the controls and crash sensor, and the radiated signal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].

bullets: Training operations conducted entirely within 50 NM of the airport where the local flights began are excepted [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].

An ELT temporarily removed for inspection, repair, modification or replacement: the records need an entry, a placard reading "ELT not installed" goes in view of the pilot, and the airplane may not be operated more than 90 days after removal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]].

callout.text: Make the ELT part of the preflight lesson: find the remote switch, read the battery date, and listen on 121.5 before shutdown after every training flight [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

check.q: What does the 12-month ELT inspection cover?
check.a: Proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and a sufficient radiated signal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].

chunks.title: Risk: low altitude, stall, spin and CFIT

body.p: Twenty percent of stall/spin accidents were preceded by engine failure [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Gliding turns need more back pressure than a straight glide, and the lighter rudder pressures without power tempt learners into too much rudder [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

bullets: A low gliding steep turn with too much rudder into the bank and added back pressure can become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Steep banks just before touchdown raise the stall speed and risk a wingtip strike [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Stretching the glide with back pressure leads to landing short and possible loss of control [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

CFIT often follows flight at night, at high density altitude, in mountainous terrain, or intentionally too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Application: a simulated approach that goes on too long becomes a real low-altitude operation.
The ACS asks applicants and instructors to recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall, spin or loss of control (ACS Appendix 2).

body.p: Collision hazards (R3): a learner spiraling over a field stares at it. The ACS expects everyone aboard to stay alert for traffic (ACS Appendix 2), and the AIH says to make the learner share responsibility for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

callout.text: You mitigate a learner's errors by flying at a safe altitude and guarding the controls, and you consciously accept the risk that remains [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

body.p: The low-altitude turn back after takeoff is taught in the Commercial lesson (CA.IX.B).

check.q: Which CFIT causes in the RMH matter for a simulated approach carried too low?
check.a: Flight at night, high density altitude, mountainous terrain, or intentionally flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

chunks.title: Risk: distraction, priorities and who is flying

bullets: Reluctance to accept the emergency shows as failure to lower the nose, delay in choosing a field, indecision, and desperate attempts to fix the problem at the expense of airplane control [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

The desire to save the airplane: a pilot conditioned in training to always find a safe area when the instructor closed the throttle may ignore basic airmanship to avoid damage, for example by stretching the glide to a nicer field. A financial stake in the airplane and the belief that no damage means no injury can feed it [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

Normal stress responses are fast and automatic, which is why emergency training must come before the emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. Over-cooperation, inappropriate laughter or very rapid mood changes under stress call for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

Confusion about who has the throttle has caused many near accidents [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Anxious learners can be very strong; when you take the controls, calmly announce "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Evaluators add realistic distractions, and failing to use sound ADM in any Task fails that Task (ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Application of the AFH 18-2 warning: do not always pull the power over a perfect field. At a safe altitude, sometimes give failures where the best option is a poor one, and talk through the least-bad touchdown.

body.p: Teaching risk in the briefing: an engine failure after takeoff is a good event for showing the learner how to assess severity in a risk matrix [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

check.q: Besides training habits, which two factors does the AFH say can feed the desire to save the airplane?
check.a: The pilot's financial stake in it and the belief that an undamaged airplane means no injury [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

body.p: Timing: introduce emergency procedures after the learner knows normal operations. Demonstrating forced landings on the first lesson can discourage and frighten a new learner [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Building blocks
Normal glide by sound, sight and feel, then abnormal glides [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]; then 90° and 180° power-off approaches, which build judgment of gliding distance [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]
Ground briefing
Who has the throttle, carb heat, where the failure will happen, how and where it ends, which items are touched and named [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Demonstration
From the right seat, fly one while you talk: best glide and trim, point out the field, the restart items, the path to the key position, the termination
Learner practice
You retard the throttle and call it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]; the learner calls each step aloud [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Scenario
Mix failures into cross-countries and other lessons; simulated emergencies and heavy workload test judgment, not only stick skill [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
End and recover
Terminate as soon as the outcome is clear [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; power at the 10 percent lead [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Debrief
Start with the learner's own assessment, then compare it with yours [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]; tie each error to its result, which is why the learner flew the first field [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]

body.p: Grade the decision-making as well as the flying: a learner who must be prompted to name the risks is at the Explain level, and one who gathers the data, weighs the options and decides without your help is at Manage/Decide [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

callout.text: On your CFI practical test you hold "Establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed, ±10 knots" (ACS AI.XII.B.S1) while explaining, and the execution must allow a safe landing if the engine really fails (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: Why mix simulated failures into cross-countries and other lessons?
check.a: Simulated emergencies and heavy workload in a planned lesson test the learner's judgment and decision-making [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

body.p: For S7 the examiner may fly errors on purpose. Name the error, say what you see, and give the fix. These come from the AFH glide, power-off approach and simulated emergency landing lists.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Eagerness to get down [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
Diving at the field, arriving at the edge too fast, floating past the spot [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
One constant glide speed; you cannot dive at a field and land on it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Not slowing to glide speed before lowering the nose [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Speed stays high, extra altitude lost
Hold altitude until best glide, then pitch and trim [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Too little back pressure at entry [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Overly steep glide right after the power cut
Counter the nose-down tendency with back pressure as the throttle closes [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Chasing the airspeed indicator [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Nose bobbing, speed never settles
Set the attitude on the horizon, trim, use sound and feel [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Stretching the glide [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Nose rising, speed decaying on an undershoot
Keep best glide; choose a closer spot [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Skidding turns to gain distance [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Ball out of center in gliding turns, too much rudder
Coordinated turns at constant bank; less rudder than with power [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Premature flaps or gear [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Configured early, then short
Full flaps only when they cannot make the airplane short [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Downwind leg stretched by a tailwind [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Long downwind, far out and low by the base key
Position the base leg for the altitude and wind, turning base in time [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Using throttle to stretch the glide [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Power added on an undershoot during practice
Throttle only to clear the engine [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Delaying the field choice [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
Circling high with no decision
General area first, then the spot [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]
Restart items forgotten [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Field chosen, no checks
Call each step aloud; build the habit until it runs during planning [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Fixing the engine at the expense of control [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
Head down in the checklist, airspeed decaying
Fly first; positive control has priority [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]

callout.text: Analyze before you correct. Was it a knowledge gap (did not know best glide), a judgment gap (late field choice) or a skill gap (chasing the airspeed)? The fix is different for each (application).

check.q: During S7 the examiner flies a long downwind, pushed by a tailwind, and ends far out and low on base. Which AFH error is it?
check.a: Overextension of the downwind leg resulting from a tailwind [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

f2.caption: Figure 3-24. Best glide speed provides the greatest forward distance. (AFH 3-22)
f2.alt: An airplane gliding toward a runway: a yellow line marked best glide speed reaches the runway, while two red lines marked too fast and too slow both reach the ground short of it.

f3.caption: Figure 9-25. Plan the base leg for wind conditions. (AFH 9-25)
f3.alt: Three airplanes fly base legs to runway 36 at different distances: in a strong wind the closest base for a steeper glide on final, in a medium wind a closer base, and in a light wind a normal base for a normal final.

f4.caption: Figure 7-12. Although carburetor ice is most likely to form when the temperature and humidity are in ranges indicated by this chart, carburetor icing is possible under conditions not depicted. (PHAK 7-10)
f4.alt: Chart of relative humidity from 50 to 100 percent against outside air temperature from 20 to 100 degrees F. A hatched box from about 20 to 70 degrees F and 80 to 100 percent humidity is labeled high carburetor icing potential; the rest of the chart is labeled carburetor icing possible.

A vertical pipe labeled net energy flow, thrust minus drag, runs down to an elevator valve between two tanks, altitude (potential energy) on the left and airspeed (kinetic energy) on the right.

scenario.title: When the simulation turns real
scenario.setup: You are instructing a private pilot learner in a carbureted, fixed-gear trainer on a cool, damp morning: 50°F and about 90 percent humidity. At 3,000 feet AGL over farmland you closed the throttle without touching the carburetor heat, and the learner flew a good glide to a large hayfield. At 700 feet AGL you call "terminate" and the learner adds full throttle. The engine coughs, runs rough, and the rpm sags well below climb power. There is no airport within gliding distance, and you are talking to no one.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause, and what goes on first?
questions.a: Carburetor ice. The day sits in the high icing potential area of the chart, and a closed throttle cools the engine and makes icing more likely. Apply full carburetor heat and leave it in full hot until normal power returns, even through roughness [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. The heat should have gone on before you closed the throttle [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

questions.q: Who flies now, and how do you make that clear?
questions.a: Take the airplane with a positive exchange: "I have the flight controls" (ACS Appendix 2), calmly, with no doubt about who is flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: The engine gives partial power. Do you use it?
questions.a: Yes, exploit whatever power the rough engine gives, but plan to switch the engine and fuel off just before touchdown if you have to land [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

questions.q: The hayfield is now behind you and a closer pasture lies ahead. Do you switch?
questions.a: Switch only for a field that is obviously better, and as a rule change your mind only once [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Keep best glide and avoid steep, low maneuvering [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

questions.q: How do you call for help?
questions.a: You are at least in an urgency condition now [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Use 121.5 MHz if you have no other frequency, MAYDAY three times if it becomes distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]], and squawk 7700 with Mode C since you cannot reach ATC right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: You land safely in the pasture. What about the ELT and what comes next?
questions.a: If a crash landing is imminent, activate the ELT if the installation permits [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]; after a normal landing, check 121.5 for an inadvertent activation and report it if found [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. Stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to think you will not be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

skills.do: From the right seat, sets the POH best glide speed promptly after the power is reduced and holds it within 10 knots either way (ACS: "Establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed, ±10 knots") while explaining the glide entry and trim.
skills.practice: Fly glide entries from cruise and from climb while talking aloud; use sound, sight and feel as your cross-check [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

skills.do: Configures the airplane per the POH/AFM and the situation: drag cleaned up for the glide, flaps and gear set for the landing at the right time, and explains why.
skills.practice: Brief each configuration change before you make it; delay full flaps until they cannot make you short [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

skills.do: Picks a suitable field within gliding distance, allowing for altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions, points it out and explains the choice.
skills.practice: On every flight, name the field you would use right now and the wind that would decide your approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

skills.do: Plans and flies straight glides or spirals to the key position and a normal power-off approach, explaining corrections for height and wind as they are made.
skills.practice: Spiral to the key position from different altitudes and over different fields so the key position never becomes a landmark [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

skills.do: Prepares for landing exactly as the evaluator specified, ends the approach at the agreed point and recovers smoothly.
skills.practice: Agree the termination and recovery before each practice; apply power at the 10 percent lead [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

skills.do: Calls the memory items and runs the restart and forced landing checklists while planning the approach, then reviews the checklist when conditions permit (ACS Appendix 2).
skills.practice: Chair-fly the POH flows until the restart items come out while you are choosing a field [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

skills.do: Watches the examiner fly deliberate errors (diving at the field, chasing the airspeed, late field choice, early flaps), names each, says what it looked like and gives the fix.
skills.practice: Have another applicant fly the errors in the AFH lists while you call them out [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: According to the CFI ACS Appendix 2, when will an evaluator ask for a simulated powerplant failure in a single-engine airplane?
options: Only above 3,000 feet AGL, over any terrain the evaluator picks
Only when the applicant has briefed the restart checklist first
Only when it is possible to safely complete a landing
Only within gliding distance of a hard-surfaced runway
quiz.why: For safety the evaluator will not request a simulated powerplant failure in a single-engine airplane unless a safe landing can be completed (ACS Appendix 2). The 3,000-foot figure belongs to multiengine shutdowns.

quiz.q: What objective does the AFH give for the simulated emergency landings an instructor gives?
options: To build accuracy, judgment, planning, procedures and confidence with little or no power
To prove the learner can restart the engine before choosing any field to land in
To show the learner that every engine failure ends in a safe landing on a good field
To give the learner practice at real off-airport landings in farm fields, pastures and on roads
quiz.why: The objective is to develop a pilot's accuracy, judgment, planning, procedures and confidence when little or no power is available [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

quiz.q: Which three airspeed references does the AFH want a learner to use consciously while learning the normal glide?
options: Airspeed indicator, VSI and altimeter
Pitch attitude, trim wheel and tachometer
Stall horn, wind noise and the airspeed indicator
Sound, visual and control pressure
quiz.why: The learner uses all three airspeed references (sound, visual and pressure) consciously until experience is gained [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: In a power-off glide, why does the AFH expect the learner to need slight left rudder?
options: Torque from the windmilling propeller grows as the airspeed slowly decays
The design compensation for p-factor and slipstream remains after they disappear
Gyroscopic precession from the slowing propeller keeps yawing the nose to the right
The left wing stalls first at best glide, so the rudder must hold it up
quiz.why: The design compensates for p-factor and slipstream under power; in a glide those effects go away but the compensation remains, so slight left rudder is likely needed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: Your learner's chosen field is poor but not a disaster. Why does the AFH have her keep flying the pattern to it until you end it?
options: It lets you explain and correct errors, and lets her see their results
Changing fields is never permitted once a field is chosen in training
The ACS fails any applicant who changes fields during the approach
A second field choice always costs more altitude than it saves
quiz.why: Normally the pilot flies to the field first chosen until the instructor ends it, so the instructor can explain and correct errors and the pilot sees their results [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. A change is permitted only when the first field would obviously end in disaster and a better one is in reach.

quiz.q: What idea about terrain does AFH chapter 18 set out to instill?
options: Only a long, flat, open field can give a survivable emergency landing
Water is always a safer choice than trees, brush or rough ground for a survivable landing
Almost any terrain can allow a survivable crash landing if the structure is used well
Terrain matters less than airspeed, so any spot will do if the touchdown is fast
quiz.why: The objective is to instill that almost any terrain can be considered suitable for a survivable crash landing if the pilot knows how to use the airplane structure for protection [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.207(b), where must a fixed automatic ELT be attached?
options: Within reach of the pilot's seat
As close to the battery as possible
On the instrument panel, near the radios
As far aft as practicable
quiz.why: Fixed and deployable automatic type transmitters must be attached as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].

quiz.q: What fraction of stall/spin accidents does the AIH say were preceded by engine failure?
options: Sixty percent
Twenty percent
Fifteen percent
Forty percent
quiz.why: Sixty percent of stall/spin accidents occurred during takeoff and landing, and twenty percent were preceded by engine failure [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: Besides LOC-I and CFIT, which two complete the RMH's top four causes of fatal general aviation accidents?
options: Midair collisions and runway incursions
Weather encounters, including thunderstorms, and wake turbulence upsets
Powerplant component failure and fuel-related issues
Fuel-related issues and gear-up landings
quiz.why: The top four are loss of control in flight, CFIT, system component failure of the powerplant, and fuel-related issues [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH want glides flown more subconsciously than other maneuvers?
options: In a forced landing, most attention goes to details other than the glide
Glides are flown only above 3,000 feet AGL, where precision matters less
A subconscious glide uses less fuel than one flown by the instruments
The examiner does not grade the glide, only the field selection and checklist
quiz.why: Most of the time during a glide in a forced landing, the pilot gives full attention to details other than the mechanics of the maneuver [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's field is a rough pasture. On final she plans to carry 10 knots extra 'for control' all the way to touchdown. What does the AFH want instead?
options: Touch down at best glide speed with the flaps up, as the POH lists for the glide
Touch down at the lowest controllable airspeed, using all available aerodynamic devices
Keep the extra 10 knots, since the float cushions the impact with the rough pasture
Any speed works, because the stopping distance and not the speed sets the severity
final_quiz.why: Speed (groundspeed) is the most critical factor in the severity of the stop, so touch down at the lowest possible controllable airspeed using all available aerodynamic devices [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks why you keep giving simulated failures she already 'knows.' Which AIH point answers her?
options: Repetition mainly keeps the instructor current for the CFI renewal requirements
Stress makes normal pilots freeze, so practice should stop the moment she feels at all nervous
The ACS sets a minimum number of simulated failures before any checkride
Under stress many responses are automatic, so training must come before the emergency
final_quiz.why: Under stress normal people respond rapidly and exactly within their training, and many responses are automatic, which is why emergency training must come before an actual emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks whether she may ever fly below best glide on a power-off approach, since you teach 'never stretch a glide.' What do the AFH pages say?
options: It may help stabilize the approach, but never to stretch a glide to reach a spot
Never: any speed below best glide is forbidden in every power-off approach
Yes, whenever she is short, because a slower speed stretches the glide farther
Only with full flaps out, which the AFH requires before flying below best glide
final_quiz.why: AFH 9-25 lists reducing airspeed below best glide among ways to stabilize the remaining approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]], while the cardinal rule forbids stretching a glide with back pressure below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: Practicing at the airport, your learner, high after a simulated failure, pushes over toward the aiming point and the VSI shows 1,400 fpm. Above what sink rate does the AFH call this excessive?
options: 300 to 400 fpm
2,000 fpm, the usual VSI limit
final_quiz.why: A sink rate in excess of 800 to 1,000 fpm is considered excessive, which is why diving at the aiming point is not a good idea [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: A simulated failure ends in a real landing at the airport. Your learner will float past her spot and starts forcing the nose down to make it. What does the AFH say?
options: Hitting the spot is the goal, so a firm push to land on it is good technique
Forcing is fine on a long runway, as long as the spot is within 200 feet
Pull the throttle further back and let the airplane settle onto the spot
Forcing it on is a listed error; a good landing past the spot beats a poor one on it
final_quiz.why: Forcing the airplane onto the runway to avoid overshooting the spot is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]; it is always better to make a good landing away from the spot than a poor one on it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

final_quiz.q: Planning a cross-country over 40 miles of forest, your learner picks the most direct line. Which AIH point fits this Task?
options: Fly the most direct route, since less time aloft means less exposure to a failure
Choose it wisely: a failure makes nearby airports and terrain supremely important
Route choice matters only at night, when the terrain below cannot be seen
Plan around airspace and TFRs; terrain is a matter for the POH, not the route
final_quiz.why: Choose the flight route wisely; an engine failure gives the nearby airports (and terrain) supreme importance [[25:10|AIH 1-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your school's registered 406 MHz ELT goes off by accident while the airplane sits in the hangar. Why does the registration matter?
options: Registration sets the 121.5 MHz homing tone so towers can find the hangar
Unregistered 406 MHz ELTs transmit only on 243.0 MHz, which very few stations ever hear
The rescue center can contact the owner, confirm the status and avoid a search
Registration replaces the 12-month inspection for the ELT under 14 CFR 91.207
final_quiz.why: Cospas-Sarsat decodes the owner data; the rescue coordination center can contact the owner to verify the status, and if the airplane is safely in a hangar a costly search is avoided [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: A real engine failure at altitude, and the propeller has stopped. On the AFH sample restart checklist, where does the ignition switch go?
options: START
BOTH
OFF, until the field is made
LEFT, then RIGHT, to find a bad magneto
final_quiz.why: The sample restart procedure lists ignition switch BOTH, or START if the propeller is stopped [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's simulated failure will end with a real landing on a long runway, and she aims for the numbers. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Aim short of the numbers so any float still lands on the runway
The numbers are best, since they leave the most runway ahead
Aim for the far end and plan to slip all the way down
Aim farther down the runway for a safety margin
final_quiz.why: Selecting the runway numbers leaves no safety cushion for a mechanical problem or misjudgment; a point farther down the runway increases the margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

final_quiz.q: Halfway down, your learner sees wires across her chosen field and a better field within gliding distance. What does the AFH say you should do?
options: Refuse; she must always fly the first field she chose
Permit the change, then explain the hazards of last-minute decisions
End the simulation at once and repeat it from the start
Take the controls and fly to the better field yourself to save time
final_quiz.why: If the first field would obviously end in disaster and a better one is within gliding distance, permit the change, then explain hazards such as excessive maneuvering at low altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

final_quiz.q: In early lessons your learner picks a good field but never gets to the restart items. How should you read this?
options: As normal early on; build the habit until checks run during planning
As a sign she is not ready for solo and should stop forced landing training
As a checklist knowledge gap only, fixed by a written test
As acceptable, since the restart items rarely work anyway
final_quiz.why: Combining emergency procedures with planning the approach is difficult early in training; the habit should develop until the critical items are checked while selecting a field [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner says, "If this were real I wouldn't bother ATC; I'd be too busy." What does the AIH ask instructors to teach?
options: That calling ATC is mainly a service for pilots on instrument flights
That an emergency must be formally declared before any rule may be broken
That declaring an emergency is appropriate and brings priority handling
That the radio call always comes before setting the best glide speed
final_quiz.why: Teach that declaring an emergency is an appropriate reaction; ATC then gives priority handling [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

final_quiz.q: Briefing a night cross-country, your learner asks where to aim if the engine quits over known, suitable terrain. Which AFH point fits?
options: Aim for the brightest lighted area nearby so you can see the ground clearly
Always land on the nearest lighted highway
Stay over the city lights until the engine restarts
Turn toward an unlighted part and consider one close to public access
final_quiz.why: Plan the landing to an unlighted portion of suitable known terrain and consider an area close to public access to help rescue [[24:230|AFH 11-13]].

takeaways: Give a simulated failure only where a safe landing could be made, and end it as soon as the outcome is clear.
Retard the throttle and call it; keep the engine warm and cleared, and settle who has the throttle before you start.
Best glide gives the most distance; hold it within ±10 knots. Minimum sink gives the most time.
Tailwind stretches the glide; land into the wind, because energy grows with the square of groundspeed.
With the engine dead the throttle no longer adds energy: one speed, spirals to the key position, then a normal power-off approach.
Teach learners to declare emergencies, use 121.5 and 7700, and know their ELT.
Vary the fields and the key position so training never promises a perfect field.
cfi_notes: For a single-engine airplane the sources describe only one way to simulate a failure: retard the throttle and call it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. The AFH mentions the mixture only for a simulated failure during a multiengine takeoff roll, and recommends a smooth throttle reduction for multiengine failures in flight below 3,000 feet AGL [[24:284|AFH 13-35]]; the zero-thrust and feathering wording in ACS Appendix 2 is also multiengine. No reference describes using the mixture, fuel selector or magnetos to fake a single-engine failure; treat that as outside the FAA guidance.

No source gives a termination altitude. The AFH says end it as soon as the outcome is known and never create undue hazard or annoyance on the ground [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; 14 CFR 91.119 gives the minimums for flight other than takeoff and landing [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. Application: since the practice ends in a go-around, plan the termination to respect those minimums. Check your school's or DPE's practice.

The AFH says keep the engine warm and cleared [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] and the PHAK says open the throttle for a few seconds periodically [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]; neither gives an interval. Brief who clears the engine so the learner does not mistake it for a restart.

AFH 9-25 lists a speed below best glide among the ways to stabilize the rest of a power-off approach, while AFH 3-23 forbids stretching a glide below best glide [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Application: they do not conflict, because a slower speed may be used to manage the approach, never to reach a field you are short of. Teach the difference explicitly.

The stabilized approach list includes a power setting not below the AFM minimum [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; it does not fit a power-off approach. The AFH itself says to focus on the elements rather than every criterion.

The 50 NM training exception in 14 CFR 91.207(f)(3) means many training airplanes may fly legally without a working ELT [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]]. Still teach every learner to find and check it, and point renters to a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
The AFH 18-2 conditioning warning is aimed at instructors: if every simulated failure ends at a perfect field, you may be training the desire to save the airplane [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].
Do not introduce forced landings on the first lesson; emergency procedures are less frightening once normal operations are familiar [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

The ACS tolerance is the same at private, commercial and CFI level (±10 knots); what changes for you is that you hold it while talking, and that you must analyze errors you see (ACS AI.XII.B.S1, AI.XII.B.S7).
gaps: Best glide speed, minimum sink speed (rarely published) and the glide ratio for your airplane come from the POH/AFM or your own flight testing.
No source gives a minimum altitude for ending a simulated forced landing; follow your school's procedures and the DPE's briefing.
No source describes simulating a single-engine failure with the mixture, fuel selector or magneto switch, or says which checklist items to move versus only touch in practice.
The sources say nothing about landowner permission or flying low over private property beyond avoiding undue hazard or annoyance [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] and the 14 CFR 91.119 minimums.
How often to clear the engine during a long glide is not stated; the POH or engine manufacturer may give guidance.

activities.title: True or false: setting it up
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH says a simulated emergency landing may be given with the airplane in any configuration.
cards.why: True. A simulated emergency landing may be given in any configuration [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

cards.s: Once you have pulled the power, a simulated approach should always continue to 500 feet AGL so the learner sees the result.
cards.why: False. It ends as soon as it can be determined whether a safe landing is assured [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

cards.s: If carburetor icing is suspected, apply full carburetor heat before closing the throttle.
cards.why: True. Heat goes full on before closed-throttle operation and stays on [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

cards.s: The simulated steps may differ somewhat from the steps used in an actual emergency.
cards.why: True, but they should be learned thoroughly and each called out [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

cards.s: Satellites still detect 121.5 MHz ELTs, so an analog unit is as fast as a 406 MHz unit.
cards.why: False. Satellite monitoring of 121.5 and 243.0 MHz ended in 2009; SAR responds to 406 MHz in minutes and to 121.5 possibly in hours [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: With the evaluator's permission, a short airborne ELT test is acceptable.
cards.why: False. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

activities.title: Glide, rules and energy
activities.intro: Work each one out, then type your answer.

items.q: Best glide gives a 700 fpm sink at 70 knots true airspeed. From 3,500 feet AGL with a 15-knot tailwind, about how far over the ground can the airplane glide, in NM?
items.why: Time aloft: 3,500 / 700 = 5 minutes. A tailwind adds groundspeed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]: 70 + 15 = 85 knots. Application: 85 x 5 / 60 = 7.08 NM, against 70 x 5 / 60 = 5.83 NM in still air.

items.q: You want to start a simulated failure over a town. The ground is at 1,150 feet MSL and the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet is a 250-foot tower. What is the lowest altitude (MSL) you may fly there?
items.why: Over a congested area: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 1,150 + 250 = 1,400 feet MSL; 1,400 + 1,000 = 2,400 feet MSL. A simulated failure there also needs terrain where a safe landing is possible (ACS Appendix 2).

items.q: Touching down at 58 knots, how many times more energy does a landing with a 12-knot tailwind carry than one into a 12-knot headwind? (One decimal.)
items.why: Kinetic energy is one half mV squared [[24:87|AFH 4-1]], so doubling groundspeed quadruples the energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Groundspeeds: 58 + 12 = 70 and 58 - 12 = 46 knots. (70 / 46) squared = 1.522 squared = 2.32.

items.q: In still air your airplane glides 8 to 1 at 69 knots true airspeed. Gliding into a 23-knot headwind, what is the glide ratio over the ground (to 1)? (One decimal.)
items.why: Glide ratio is distance forward compared with height lost [[24:82|AFH 3-21]], and a headwind shortens the glide because the groundspeed is lower [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Application: the sink rate is unchanged, so distance scales with groundspeed: 69 - 23 = 46 knots; 8 x 46 / 69 = 5.33 to 1.

items.q: Your POH best glide speed is 68 KIAS. What is the lowest indicated airspeed that still meets the ACS standard for this Task?
items.why: "Establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed, ±10 knots" (ACS AI.XII.B.S1): 68 - 10 = 58 knots.

activities.title: Your learner's first simulated forced landing
activities.intro: You are the CFI. Your private pilot learner is in a carbureted, fixed-gear trainer at 3,500 feet AGL on a cool, humid morning (55°F, 85 percent humidity). Farmland lies west, a small town east. Today is her first simulated engine failure at altitude, and you have briefed that you will handle the throttle.

steps.s: Where and how do you start the simulated failure?
options: Over the town, so she has to search hard for a field
Over the farmland, after clearing turns and with carburetor heat full on before you close the throttle
Over the farmland, closing the throttle first and adding carb heat only if the engine roughens
Over a large lake, so there is no obvious field to make it harder
steps.why: A simulated failure is given only where a safe landing is possible (ACS Appendix 2); clear the area first [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; on a humid day carb heat goes full on before the throttle closes [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

steps.s: You close the throttle and call it. She is 30 knots above best glide and pushes the nose straight down. What do you say?
options: "Good, get the nose down fast"
"Lower flaps to slow down"
"Climb steeply to save altitude"
"Hold altitude until best glide, then pitch and trim"
steps.why: Above best glide, let it slow (even climb) to best glide, then lower the nose and trim [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]; not slowing first is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

steps.s: She picks a good field, then dives into the restart checklist. The airspeed is now 15 knots below best glide. What do you do?
options: Let her finish the checklist; airspeed comes second
Take the controls and end the lesson for today
Say "airspeed" and have her fly the glide first, checklist as workload allows
Pull the checklist out of her hands without a word
steps.why: Fixing the problem at the expense of airplane control is a classic error [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]; positive control comes first [[24:353|AFH 18-4]], and she is outside the ±10-knot standard (ACS AI.XII.B.S1).

steps.s: She reaches the key position about 300 feet high with the whole field ahead. What now?
options: Let her fix it with a slip, flaps or a wider base and keep flying
End the simulation; a high approach cannot be saved
Tell her to dive at the aiming point
Have her retract the flaps
steps.why: Slips, flaps, base leg placement and the turn to final correct misjudged height [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]; you cannot dive at a field and land on it [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

steps.s: At 600 feet AGL the landing is clearly assured. Cattle graze near a farmhouse at the far end of the field. What do you do?
options: Continue to 50 feet to prove she would have made it
Terminate now and recover with power at the 10 percent lead
Land in the field to show her it works
Continue to 200 feet and then decide
steps.why: End as soon as a safe landing is known to be assured, without undue hazard or annoyance to people or property [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; add power slowly but positively at the 10 percent lead [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
